title: Primal-Dual Flow Matching for Sample-Wise Constrained Generation

paper.title: Primal-Dual Flow Matching for Sample-Wise Constrained Generation
paper.abstract: Abstract We consider the problem of learning to generate data while satisfying a prescribed sample-wise constraint with a user-specified probability of constraint satisfaction. Starting with a population-level constrained negative log-likelihood minimization and using a flow-matching (FM) parameterization, under regularity assumptions and sufficient expressivity of the velocity field family, we derive guarantees on the probability of constraint satisfaction for the corresponding primal-dual optimization algorithm. We provide a practical implementation of this approach, called Primal-Dual Flow Matching (PDFM), which has direct control over constraint satisfaction rate and requires only binary membership oracle feedback for constraint satisfaction, avoiding the need for differentiable distances, projections, or special structure of the constraint set, such as convexity. We show that PDFM improves constraint satisfaction over vanilla FM and achieves competitive performance against constraint-aware baselines while maintaining distributional fidelity. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZhengyanHuan/PDFM .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The utility of generative models for scientific applications highly depends on their ability to generate samples that obey scientific laws or satisfy an application-specific criterion, modeled via constraints that can be validated numerically. For example, flow- and diffusion-based generative models are increasingly used to emulate chaotic spatiotemporal systems ( Lienen et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Price et al., 2025 ) , where the chaotic dynamics result in high sensitivity to initial conditions and therefore unpredictable trajectories that can be interpreted and modeled probabilistically ( Medio and Lines, 2001 ) . However, in these settings, distributional fidelity alone is rarely sufficient: a generated sample is useful only if it is also physically consistent , e.g., satisfying boundary conditions, respecting conservation laws, or following a governing PDE ( Beucler et al., 2021 ; Utkarsh et al., 2025 ) . Another important example comes from molecular generation ( Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ) , where one wants to generate new molecules such that they conform to structures with chemically useful properties ( Bickerton et al., 2012 ; Giaginis et al., 2018 ) that are numerically quantifiable.

sections.heading: Related work:
sections.text: For constrained generation, one may divide existing literature into (a) Type of constraints, e.g., distributional constraints ( Khalafi et al., 2024 ) or sample-wise constraints [this work]. Among sample-wise constraints, one may have constraints with topological specification, such as convexity ( Liu et al., 2023 ) ; constraints with known boundaries ( Lou and Ermon, 2023 ; Fishman et al., 2023 ) ; constraints with differentiable distances to them ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Utkarsh et al., 2025 ) ; or constraints that are known only via a membership oracle ( Huan et al., 2026 ) ; and (b) Methods used – whether it is inference-time ( Christopher et al., 2024 ) ( Utkarsh et al., 2025 ) ( Li et al., 2026 ) ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) or training-time [this work], ( Lou and Ermon, 2023 ; Fishman et al., 2023 ) ( Xie et al., 2024 ) ( Feng et al., 2025 ) ( Giannone et al., 2023 ) ( Huan et al., 2026 ) . A more detailed review of these related works is provided in Appendix A and throughout the exposition we will highlight other closely related works. For sample-wise constrained generation when the constraints are accessible via a membership oracle, we make the following main contributions : 1. We develop a theoretically grounded approach, with provable guarantees on the probability of constraint satisfaction. In particular, leveraging an FM parameterization of a constrained negative log-likelihood minimization (Sections 2 , 3 ), in Theorem 3.5 we show that under mild assumptions the Total Variation (TV) norm between the optimal solution and the FM parameterized solution can be controlled in terms of approximation error between the flows due to parametric modeling, which in turn leads to overall control on constraint satisfaction. We then show that a theoretical Primal-Dual Flow Matching (PDFM) Alg. 1 achieves this bound. 2. We then propose a practical implementation of PDFM in Alg. 2 , with theoretical guarantees discussed in Sec. 4.3 . Key innovations in this algorithm are motivated by deterministic policy gradient methods, where we build differentiable surrogates for constraint satisfaction probability under the FM parameterization. This enables the method to work with only membership oracle access to the constraint set. We note that this type of access to the constraint is the most flexible when the constraints are complex. 3. We provide an extensive evaluation of PDFM and show that compared to existing methods, it achieves competitive constraint satisfaction rates and distribution fidelity. For scientific applications, we consider the problem of learning to generate PDE-constrained spatiotemporal dynamics of chaotic systems and show that our method achieves superior performance while requiring only binary feedback. In a molecule generation task, PDFM improves molecule stability and distributional fidelity over FM over FM, without task-specific designs.

5.1 Illustrative 2 2 -D Constrained Generation ( Q ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) < b Q(\mathcal{C})<b )
sections.text: We begin with a synthetic 2 2 -D constrained generation example. Let z = ( z 1 , z 2 ) ∈ ℝ 2 z=(z_{1},z_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2} denote a sample. The clean distribution is a uniform distribution over two disconnected regions, 𝒞 = { ( z 1 , z 2 ) : 1 ≤ | z 1 | ≤ 5 , 1 ≤ | z 2 | ≤ 5 , z 1 z 2 > 0 } . \mathcal{C}=\{(z_{1},z_{2}):1\leq|z_{1}|\leq 5,\;1\leq|z_{2}|\leq 5,\;z_{1}z_{2}>0\}. Samples from the clean distribution are corrupted by additive zero-mean Gaussian noise with variance 0.01 0.01 , yielding the training distribution Q Q , for which Q ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) ≈ 96 % Q(\mathcal{C})\approx 96\% . Following the formulation in ( OPT ), the goal is to learn a distribution that remains as close as possible to Q Q while achieving a constraint satisfaction rate of at least b = 99.5 % b=99.5\% . We compare PDFM against two FM-based baselines: (1) vanilla FM trained on samples from Q Q ; and (2) FM trained on the truncated distribution Q ′ = Q ( ⋅ ∣ 𝒞 ) Q^{\prime}=Q(\cdot\mid\mathcal{C}) , obtained by discarding infeasible training samples, with density q ′ ​ ( x ) = q ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝟏 𝒞 ​ ( x ) / Q ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) q^{\prime}(x)={q(x)\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}}(x)}/{Q(\mathcal{C})} . The visualization of the clean distribution, Q Q , P ( λ ∗ ) P^{(\lambda^{*})} (computed for this simple case via Lemma 2.2 ), the distributions induced by baselines (1), (2), and PDFM are shown in Appendix H.1 Fig. 1 . We evaluate two metrics: the constraint satisfaction rate and the Sliced Wasserstein Distance (SWD) ( Bonneel et al., 2014 ) between samples from the trained model and samples from P ( λ ∗ ) P^{(\lambda^{*})} . SWD measures distributional similarity, with smaller values indicating better similarity. Reported metrics use 50000 50000 generated samples, averaged over 100 100 trials. Baseline (1) shows that vanilla FM trained directly on Q Q produces a distribution with constraint satisfaction rate 96.37 % 96.37\% , close to Q ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) Q(\mathcal{C}) , but below the target level b = 99.5 % b=99.5\% ; its SWD is 0.1384 0.1384 . Baseline (2) shows that even when FM is trained on the truncated distribution, whose training samples are all feasible, it still fails to fully enforce the constraint, achieving constraint satisfaction rate 98.74 % 98.74\% and SWD 0.1156 0.1156 . In this synthetic example, discarding infeasible samples removes only about 4 % 4\% of the data; in more realistic settings, as shown in Sec. 5.3 , this rejection step can discard a much larger fraction of the training set and thereby degrade distributional matching . In contrast, PDFM achieves the target constraint level, with a constraint satisfaction rate 99.51 % 99.51\% , while also attaining the lowest SWD, 0.1096 0.1096 . We therefore conclude that, with samples from Q Q , PDFM achieves better constraint satisfaction than FM baselines trained on either Q Q or the truncated distribution Q ′ Q^{\prime} , while attaining superior distributional fidelity.

sections.text: We next evaluate PDFM on higher-dimensional synthetic tasks in this regime, together with several baselines, MDM ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , NAMM ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , PDM ( Christopher et al., 2024 ) , PCFM ( Utkarsh et al., 2025 ) , and FM-RE ( Huan et al., 2026 ) , introduced in Appendix A . The target distribution Q Q is a Gaussian mixture model, with a constraint defined as an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} ball constraint 𝒞 = { x ∈ ℝ d | ‖ x ‖ 2 ≤ 1 } \mathcal{C}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\Big|\|x\|_{2}\leq 1\right\} . Specifically, we consider d d isotropic Gaussians, each with variance 0.05 0.05 , centered at each of the d d standard unit vectors, and reject samples outside 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , i.e., Q ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) = 1 Q(\mathcal{C})=1 . This setting is also considered in Liu et al. (2023) . FM achieves P ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) = 97.633 % P(\mathcal{C})=97.633\% and 90.918 % 90.918\% in the 8-D and 20-D cases, respectively, showing that constrained generation remains nontrivial even when Q ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) ≥ b Q(\mathcal{C})\geq b , in which case the population-level optimum is Q Q . For a direct comparison with FM-RE ( Huan et al., 2026 ) , which also relies on membership oracle feedback, we set the target constraint satisfaction rate b b to match the P ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) P(\mathcal{C}) attained by FM-RE, namely b = 99.923 % b=99.923\% for the 8 8 -D case and b = 99.748 % b=99.748\% for the 20 20 -D case. The results in Table 1 show that PDFM achieves P ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) P(\mathcal{C}) close to the target b b while yielding a smaller SWD than FM-RE, demonstrating superior performance in both constraint satisfaction and distributional matching. It is worth noting that PDFM can be configured to match the constraint satisfaction level achieved by FM-RE, whereas the reverse is not straightforward. The reason is that PDFM directly controls P ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) P(\mathcal{C}) through b b , while FM-RE can only influence P ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) P(\mathcal{C}) indirectly by adjusting the weight of the constraint term. Therefore, compared with FM-RE, PDFM substantially reduces the burden of hyperparameter tuning. Compared with MDM, which requires convexity and a special structure of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , NAMM and PCFM, which both require a differentiable distance to 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , and PDM, which requires projection onto 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , PDFM works with arguably the most flexible requirement on the constraint set specification: access via a membership oracle. Despite this weaker requirement, PDFM achieves strong constraint satisfaction while maintaining competitive distributional fidelity. sections.heading: 5.3 Unconditional PDE-Constrained Generation of Spatiotemporal Dynamics
sections.text: A central challenge in applying generative modeling to applications involving dynamical systems, including chaotic systems, is generating samples that respect known physical laws such as the underlying governing equations. We illustrate PDFM on the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (KS) equation, a canonical model of spatiotemporal chaos ( Kuramoto and Tsuzuki, 1976 ; Sivashinsky, 1977 ) , where the constraint set 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is defined by the residual of generated space-time patches against the numerical PDE solver. This setting is representative of generative emulation tasks in which a forward solver can evaluate whether a sample obeys the dynamics. Given a dataset of non-overlapping space–time patches x ∈ ℝ 64 × 64 x\in\mathbb{R}^{64\times 64} , the objective is to learn a generative model that produces patches satisfying the KS dynamics up to a prescribed tolerance with a user-specified probability. Specifically, a forward solver, which is assumed to be non-differentiable , provides the residual feedback δ L n \delta_{L_{n}} , where δ L n = 0 \delta_{L_{n}}=0 indicates strict alignment with the KS dynamics up to solver precision. A sample is considered feasible if δ L n < τ \delta_{L_{n}}<\tau , where τ \tau denotes the prescribed error tolerance. Details of the dataset construction and residual computation are provided in Appendix H.3 . Two generation cases are considered.

sections.heading: Case 1:
sections.text: The clean patches x ∈ ℝ 64 × 64 x\in\mathbb{R}^{64\times 64} with δ L n = 0 \delta_{L_{n}}=0 from the solver are used as the training data. The threshold is τ = 0.033 \tau=0.033 , and the target constraint satisfaction rate is 98 % 98\% . In this case, all samples from the training distribution satisfy the constraints, indicating Q ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) = 1 Q(\mathcal{C})=1 .

Specifically, for each sample, along the spatial dimension, every 9 9 -th position is replaced by a linearly interpolated value between the adjacent values. This leads to an average δ L n = 0.0555 \delta_{L_{n}}=0.0555 for the training samples. Although FM ( Q ′ ) (Q^{\prime}) improves the constraint satisfaction rate from 9.82 % 9.82\% for FM ( Q ) (Q) to 33.24 % 33.24\% , it remains far below the target rate of 90 % 90\% . Moreover, fewer training samples lead to a degraded generated distribution, as reflected by the increased histogram error. The results in Table 2 illustrate four properties of PDFM that are particularly relevant in this setting. First, even when the training distribution itself satisfies the constraint perfectly (Case 1, Q ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) = 1 Q(\mathcal{C})=1 ), vanilla FM only achieves P ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) = 14.19 % P(\mathcal{C})=14.19\% , confirming that local consistency does not transfer for free from the training distribution to the trained model; PDFM raises this rate to 97.74 % 97.74\% at the prescribed target while keeping the marginal summary statistics close to the training data. Second, in the more realistic Case 2 with degraded training data ( Q ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) ≈ 39.47 % Q(\mathcal{C})\approx 39.47\% ), PDFM closes the gap from 9.82 % / 33.24 % 9.82\%/33.24\% to 90.48 % 90.48\% , demonstrating that the chance-constrained formulation lets the generative model produce samples of higher dynamical quality than the data it was trained on, by leveraging the solver-based residual oracle to suppress non-physical regions of the learned distribution. Third, while PCFM and NAMM, requiring the fully differentiable residual, fail in this task, PDFM reaches these satisfaction rates without differentiating through the numerical stepper, which is essential when the stepper is non-differentiable, written in a legacy language, or otherwise available only as a black box. Fourth, compared with FM-RE, which also requires only membership oracle feedback, PDFM provides direct control over the constraint satisfaction rate and can therefore target a prescribed feasibility level rather than relying on an implicitly tuned penalty weight.

sections.heading: 5.4 Additional Applications
sections.text: Fingerprint image generation. We further evaluate PDFM on SOCOFing fingerprint ( Shehu et al., 2018 ) generation with a ridge-connectivity constraint, assessed by a non-differentiable image-processing oracle. The oracle applies thresholding and skeletonization, then checks whether the number of connected ridge components is below a prescribed threshold. PDFM achieves a mean constraint satisfaction rate of 99.28 % 99.28\% , meeting the target b = 99 % b=99\% , compared with 72.74 % 72.74\% for FM and 88.14 % 88.14\% for FM-RE. Meanwhile, PDFM maintains NLLs comparable to FM and preserves visual fidelity. Experimental details and sample visualizations are provided in Appendix H.4 . 3 3 -D molecule generation. Trained on QM9 ( Ramakrishnan et al., 2014 ) , we aim to generate samples satisfying a molecule-stability constraint requiring all atoms to satisfy valid valency rules after bond inference. Using only binary feasibility feedback for constraint satisfaction, PDFM improves the mean molecule stability rate from 32.77 % 32.77\% to 48.75 % 48.75\% and reduces NLL from − 19.74 -19.74 to − 20.70 -20.70 relative to FM. Although the stability rate remains below the target b = 60 % b=60\% , these results demonstrate both improved feasibility and improved likelihood quality, without task-specific designs. Further details are provided in Appendix H.5 .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we present PDFM, a primal-dual framework for constrained generation that requires only membership oracle feedback, provides direct control over the constraint satisfaction rate, and admits theoretical guarantees. We also propose a non-stochastic constraint-guided approach for updating the velocity field, enabling efficient use of oracle feedback during primal optimization. One of the limitations of PDFM arises from the need to obtain sufficient positive constraint satisfaction feedback during training to learn f ϕ f_{\phi} reliably. Further details are discussed in Appendix I .

sections.heading: Appendix A Related work
sections.text: Constrained generative modeling has been studied from several complementary perspectives, depending on whether the constraint is imposed at the distribution level or at the level of individual generated samples. We refer to these two settings as distributional constraints and sample-wise constraints , respectively. This paper investigates sample-wise constraints with the objective of generating samples within the constraint set 𝒞 \mathcal{C} . A closely related work of constrained generative models in the domain of distributional constraints is Khalafi et al. [2024] , which requires the generated distribution to remain close in KL divergence, to one or more reference distributions. While Khalafi et al. [2024] and this work both utilize primal-dual frameworks for constrained generative modeling, their scopes and theoretical guarantees differ substantially due to different constraint settings. Algorithmically, this work’s optimization strategy designed for sample-wise constraints in Sec. 4.2 deviates from the score/flow loss in classical generative models. For sample-wise constraints, existing approaches can be broadly divided into training-time and inference-time methods . Training-time methods incorporate constraint information during model training, for example, by modifying the objective, architecture, or learned dynamics. This typically requires additional training effort, but they can generally use standard/slightly-modified sampling procedures at inference time. In contrast, inference-time methods can often be applied to regularly trained generative models, but they must steer, project, or correct the sampling trajectory during generation, which usually increases inference-time computational cost. This paper is a training-time method , that informs the FM model of the constraints during training and uses standard Euler sampling with the learned velocity field.

sections.heading: A.1 Training-Time Methods
sections.text: Among training-time methods assuming Q ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) = 1 Q(\mathcal{C})=1 , approaches that enforce strict feasibility of the generated samples, i.e., P ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) = 1 P(\mathcal{C})=1 , generally require stronger structures and knowledge of the constraint set 𝒞 \mathcal{C} . Reflection-based methods, such as the reflected diffusion model (RDM) [ Lou and Ermon, 2023 , Fishman et al., 2023 ] and reflected flow matching (RFM) [ Xie et al., 2024 ] enforce constraint satisfaction via reflected generation trajectories within 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , requiring convexity of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} and explicit knowledge of the constraint boundary ∂ 𝒞 \partial\mathcal{C} . Mirror-based approaches, such as mirror diffusion model (MDM) [ Liu et al., 2023 ] , enforce constraint satisfaction by performing DDPM training in the domain of an unconstrained mapping of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , and obtaining generated samples from the inverse mapping of the unconstrained domain. MDM requires convexity of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} and an available closed-form bijective mapping between 𝒞 \mathcal{C} and the unconstrained space. Convexity of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , boundary information, and tractable bijective maps are often unavailable for complex constraints in practical settings. To broaden applicability, several existing methods relax strict feasibility guarantees and instead aim to improve, but not necessarily ensure, constraint satisfaction. Neural approximate mirror map (NAMM) [ Feng et al., 2025 ] aims to approximate the bijective projection in MDM via NNs, relaxing the requirement of convexity and a closed-form bijective map to a differentiable distance to 𝒞 \mathcal{C} . Trajectory Alignment [ Giannone et al., 2023 ] trains diffusion models to align their sampling paths with the intermediate iterates of a physics-based optimizer, improving constrained design generation but requiring access to optimizer-generated trajectories during training. Flow Matching with Random Exploration (FM-RE) [ Huan et al., 2026 ] improves feasibility by adding an explicit constraint-aware term to the FM training objective and injecting Gaussian noise into the generation trajectories to enable likelihood-ratio gradient estimation, thereby requiring only membership oracle feedback for 𝒞 \mathcal{C} . However, FM-RE’s P ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) P(\mathcal{C}) is only implicitly controlled by the weight of the constraint-aware term, and FM-RE does not provide a theoretical guarantee for feasibility. PDFM improves upon FM-RE while retaining the same weak requirement of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , i.e., membership oracle access, and further provides theoretical guarantees and direct control over the constraint satisfaction rate P ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) P(\mathcal{C}) .

sections.heading: A.2 Inference-Time Methods
sections.text: Inference-time methods improve or enforce constraint satisfaction by modifying the sampling procedure of a pretrained generative model, typically through guidance, projection, or trajectory correction during generation. Projected diffusion model (PDM) [ Christopher et al., 2024 ] enforces strict feasibility by repeatedly projecting stochastic diffusion updates onto 𝒞 \mathcal{C} at each step, requiring an available projection function, and potentially causing deviations from the training distribution. Physics-constrained flow matching (PCFM) [ Utkarsh et al., 2025 ] enforces constraints through forward-shooting and Gauss–Newton correction of predicted terminal states, which requires a differentiable constraint residual and access to its Jacobian. HardFlow [ Li et al., 2026 ] enforces hard constraints by reformulating FM sampling as a trajectory-optimization problem, requiring an explicit constraint function and a tractable constrained-optimization solver during sampling. Doob-Oriented Inference-time Transformation (DOIT) [ Zhu et al., 2026 ] improves constraint satisfaction by applying Doob’s h h -transform to add a dynamic correction to the diffusion sampling process, which can handle non-differentiable reward feedback but requires Monte Carlo reward-query estimates during sampling. While inference-time methods avoid retraining, they typically require a nontrivial design of the guidance, correction, or optimization procedure and impose additional computational burden during sampling.

sections.heading: Dataset construction and residual computation:
sections.text: We construct a dataset of Kuramoto–Sivashinsky dynamics by numerically solving the conservative PDE with fixed solver parameters and randomly sampled truncated-Fourier initial conditions, using Exponax [ Koehler et al., 2024 ] . From each long trajectory, we extract non-overlapping space–time patches x ∈ ℝ d × d x\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} , where x [ : , i ] x[:,i] denotes the spatial state at time index i i . Let F ⁡ ( ⋅ ) F(\cdot) denote one application of the numerical stepper. Let x ^ \hat{x} denote the generated sample, and for each i = 0 , … , d − 2 i=0,\dots,d-2 , we regard x ^ [ : , i ] \hat{x}[:,i] as the true current state, compute the next true state x [ : , i + 1 ] = F ( x ^ [ : , i ] ) {x}[:,{i+1}]=F(\hat{x}[:,i]) , and compare it with the next estimated state x ^ [ : , i + 1 ] \hat{x}[:,i+1] , yielding the residual r i = x [ : , i + 1 ] − x ^ [ : , i + 1 ] r_{i}=x[:,i+1]-\hat{x}[:,{i+1}] . The resulting residual sequence { r i } i = 0 d − 2 \{r_{i}\}_{i=0}^{d-2} defines the size-normalized residual δ L n := ( 1 ( d − 1 ) ​ d ​ ∑ i = 0 d − 2 ‖ r i ‖ n n ) 1 / n \delta_{L_{n}}:=\left(\frac{1}{(d-1)d}\sum_{i=0}^{d-2}\|r_{i}\|_{n}^{n}\right)^{1/n} , with the usual extension for n = ∞ n=\infty . A generated sample is defined as satisfying the constraint if δ L n < τ \delta_{L_{n}}<\tau , in which τ \tau is a prescribed tolerance. In this task, we set d = 64 , n = 1 d=64,n=1 .

sections.heading: Network architectures:
sections.text: The velocity network u θ u_{\theta} takes x t ∈ ℝ 1 × 64 × 64 x_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 64\times 64} and the time t ∈ ℝ t\in\mathbb{R} as inputs. A 128 128 -dimensional sinusoidal time embedding is projected to dimension 256 256 , while x t x_{t} is projected to 64 64 channels. The network then applies five residual space-time blocks, each combining 5 × 1 5\times 1 spatial, 1 × 5 1\times 5 physical-time, and 3 × 3 3\times 3 joint convolutions with group normalization, SiLU activations, and time-conditioned transformations. A final 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution produces u θ ​ ( x t , t ) ∈ ℝ 1 × 64 × 64 u_{\theta}(x_{t},t)\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 64\times 64} . The feasibility predictor uses the same backbone with separate parameters, followed by global average pooling, a scalar linear output, and a sigmoid function producing f ϕ ​ ( x t , t ) ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) f_{\phi}(x_{t},t)\in(0,1) .

sections.text: for both cases, learning rate for the velocity field η ( θ ) = 1 × 10 − 5 \eta^{(\theta)}=1\times 10^{-5} , learning rate for the classifier η ( ϕ ) = 1 × 10 − 4 \eta^{(\phi)}=1\times 10^{-4} , dual variable learning rate η i = 2 \eta_{i}=2 .

sections.heading: Significance for chaotic PDE emulation.
sections.text: The Kuramoto–Sivashinsky setting is representative of generative emulation tasks for chaotic systems, where samples are drawn from the emergent chaotic attractor. High-quality emulation requires both local dynamical accuracy and statistical fidelity to that attractor. The two terms in the PDFM objective parallel this decomposition: the FM loss matches the attractor distribution, while the chance constraint enforces local consistency with the dynamics, providing a principled probabilistic alternative to the combination of next-step prediction error and statistical-fidelity losses common in deterministic emulators of chaotic systems [ Jiang et al., 2023 , Melo et al., 2026 ] . To quantify the discrepancy between generated samples and the simulator predictions, we extract the first column of each generated sample as the initial state and use the simulator to predict the subsequent 63 63 states. sections.heading: H.4 SOCOFing Fingerprint Generation with Ridge-Connectivity Constraint
sections.text: We consider the task of generating fingerprint images with a ridge-connectivity constraint, using the Sokoto Coventry Fingerprint Dataset (SOCOFing) [ Shehu et al., 2018 ] for training. SOCOFing is a public grayscale fingerprint image dataset containing real fingerprint samples and synthetically altered variants. It includes fingerprints collected from multiple subjects and provides altered versions with varying levels of distortion. Collected fingerprint images and the altered variants can be corrupted by sensor noise, partial occlusion, pressure variation, or preprocessing artifacts, which may break continuous ridge structures into disconnected fragments. We therefore consider a ridge-connectivity constraint, which requires the main fingerprint ridges to remain sufficiently continuous; satisfying this constraint indicates that the image preserves coherent ridge structure. Concretely, we evaluate this constraint using a non-differentiable image-processing oracle. For each grayscale fingerprint image, we first apply Otsu thresholding to separate ridge pixels from the background, treating ridges as the foreground. We then skeletonize the foreground ridge map into a one-pixel-wide representation and count the number of connected components in the skeletonized image. A sample is considered feasible if the number of connected ridge components is below the prescribed threshold 50 50 . We use the Real and Altered-Easy partitions of the SOCOFing as the training set. Among the 23931 23931 training samples, 16235 16235 of them satisfy this ridge-connectivity constraint, indicating Q ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) ≈ 67.84 % Q(\mathcal{C})\approx 67.84\% . The target constraint satisfaction rate is set to b = 99 % b=99\% .

sections.heading: Network architectures:
sections.text: The velocity network takes x t ∈ ℝ 1 × 96 × 96 x_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 96\times 96} and t ∈ ℝ t\in\mathbb{R} as inputs. It uses a four-level U-Net with channel dimensions 64 64 , 128 128 , 256 256 , and 512 512 , three downsampling and three upsampling layers, skip connections, and two residual blocks at the bottleneck. A 256 256 -dimensional sinusoidal embedding of t t is projected and added to the features in each residual block. A final 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution produces u θ ​ ( x t , t ) ∈ ℝ 1 × 96 × 96 u_{\theta}(x_{t},t)\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 96\times 96} . The feasibility predictor uses a three-level encoder with channel dimensions 64 64 , 128 128 , and 256 256 , followed by two residual blocks, global average pooling, and a sigmoid output f ϕ ​ ( x t , t ) ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) f_{\phi}(x_{t},t)\in(0,1) .

sections.text: learning rate for the velocity field η ( θ ) = 1 × 10 − 5 \eta^{(\theta)}=1\times 10^{-5} , learning rate for the classifier η ( ϕ ) = 1 × 10 − 4 \eta^{(\phi)}=1\times 10^{-4} , dual variable learning rate η i = 5 \eta_{i}=5 . For this oracle-constrained task, only constraint-aware methods compatible with membership oracle feedback are applicable. Therefore, we compare PDFM against FM-RE and the vanilla FM baseline. The performances are evaluated in two aspects: constraint satisfaction rate and negative log-likelihood (NLL). NLL is computed by treating the finite-step sampler as a sequence of invertible transformations from a base noise distribution to the data space. For each evaluation sample, the discrete updates are inverted to recover the corresponding latent noise, the log density of this latent under the base distribution is evaluated, and the log-determinant correction associated with each discrete transformation is accumulated to obtain the sample log likelihood; the NLL is then the negative average log likelihood over the evaluation set. Lower NLL indicates that the model assigns a higher probability density to the evaluated samples under this discrete likelihood. In this setting, we estimate NLL using 100 100 Euler discretization steps on two evaluation sets: the full training set, denoted by 𝒟 train \mathcal{D_{\mathrm{train}}} , which includes both feasible and infeasible samples, and the feasible subset { x ∈ D train : x ∈ 𝒞 } \{x\in D_{\mathrm{train}}:x\in\mathcal{C}\} , obtained by discarding infeasible samples. We report these as NLL train \mathrm{NLL}_{\mathrm{train}} and NLL feas \mathrm{NLL}_{\mathrm{feas}} , respectively. PDFM successfully achieves the target constraint satisfaction rate of 99 % 99\% , while maintaining NLLs comparable to those of FM. The generated samples from FM-RE display a slightly perturbed background, indicating a degraded induced distribution. PDFM and FM generate samples that are visually close to the training samples. This further validates that PDFM is able to achieve the desired feasibility control while preserving distributional quality and visual fidelity. sections.heading: H.5 QM9 3 3 -D Molecule Generation
sections.text: We evaluate PDFM on 3 3 -D molecule generation using the QM9 dataset [ Ramakrishnan et al., 2014 ] , a standard benchmark of small organic molecules with atom types and 3 3 -D coordinates. This task is important for the discovery of new drug molecules. The molecules are represented as ( x , h ) (x,h) , in which x x represents the 3 3 -D atom coordinates and h h contains atom features such as atom types and charges. Here, the sample-wise constraint is molecule stability: a generated molecule is considered feasible if its atoms satisfy valid valency rules after bond inference, so that the generated structure is chemically stable at the atom level. In this dataset, 95.2 % 95.2\% of the samples are stable, indicating Q ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) ≈ 95.2 % Q(\mathcal{C})\approx 95.2\% . Note that the stability constraint is a membership oracle constraint, without differentiable distances to the feasible set or available projections. Existing works such as [ Song et al., 2023 ] introduce molecule-specific architectural and training designs, including hybrid probability paths for coordinates x x and atom features h h , equivariant optimal transport for coordinates, Hungarian–Kabsch alignment, and information-aligned paths for atom features, achieving superior stability rates. In this section, we investigate whether PDFM can improve constraint satisfaction using only binary feasibility feedback, without relying on such domain-specific knowledge.

sections.heading: Network architectures.
sections.text: Following the EGNN backbone of Satorras et al. [2021] , each molecular state x t ∈ ℝ N × 8 x_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 8} is represented as a graph with three coordinates and five atom features per node. For both FM and PDFM, the velocity network uses four time-conditioned EGNN blocks with hidden dimension 64 64 , where pairwise relative coordinates and distances are used to update node features and coordinates. A 64 64 -dimensional sinusoidal embedding of t t conditions each block, and the network outputs u θ ​ ( x t , t ) ∈ ℝ N × 8 u_{\theta}(x_{t},t)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 8} . The feasibility predictor uses a separate pairwise graph network with hidden dimension 128 128 , a 32 32 -dimensional time embedding, and two interaction blocks. Pairwise messages are constructed from node features, relative coordinates, and squared distances and are aggregated by averaging. The pooled graph representation and summary statistics of pairwise distances are passed through an MLP and a sigmoid function to produce f ϕ ​ ( x t , t ) ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) f_{\phi}(x_{t},t)\in(0,1) .

sections.text: learning rate for the velocity field η ( θ ) = 1 × 10 − 5 \eta^{(\theta)}=1\times 10^{-5} , learning rate for the classifier η ( ϕ ) = 1 × 10 − 4 \eta^{(\phi)}=1\times 10^{-4} , dual variable learning rate η i = 10 \eta_{i}=10 . Following EDM [ Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ] , we use NLL as a likelihood-based measure of distributional alignment 𝔼 x ∼ Q ​ [ − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( x ) ] \mathbb{E}_{x\sim Q}[-\log p_{\theta}(x)] , together with molecule stability to evaluate sample-wise chemical feasibility. Lower NLL indicates that the model assigns a larger probability density to the observed data and therefore achieves a better distributional match. In practice, NLL is approximated with a finite-step Euler sampler by reversing the discrete updates to recover the latent noise, evaluating its prior probability, and accumulating each step’s density/volume-change correction. In this task, NLL is evaluated using 100 100 discrete steps. The visualizations of the generated samples are provided in Fig. 9 and Fig. 10 . Over 10 10 trials, constraint satisfaction is evaluated using 1000 1000 generated samples per trial, while NLL is evaluated using 100 100 randomly selected samples from the training set per trial. FM achieves P ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) = ( 32.77 ± 1.22 ) % P(\mathcal{C})=(32.77\pm 1.22)\% and NLL = − 19.74 ± 0.44 \mathrm{NLL}=-19.74\pm 0.44 . PDFM, trained with the target b = 60 % b=60\% , achieves P ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) = ( 48.75 ± 1.56 ) % P(\mathcal{C})=(48.75\pm 1.56)\% and NLL = − 20.70 ± 0.25 \mathrm{NLL}=-20.70\pm 0.25 . Results are reported as the mean and standard deviation. While PDFM is unable to achieve the target constraint satisfaction rate due to the design limitations, including the generic backbone and probability path without domain-specific knowledge, it substantially improves constraint satisfaction over the FM baseline. Moreover, the improvement is achieved without sacrificing likelihood quality: PDFM obtains a lower NLL, indicating higher distributional alignment with the training distribution. This suggests that PDFM is able to improve constraint satisfaction while preserving, or even improving, distributional fidelity without task-specific designs and with only membership oracle feedback.

sections.heading: I.1 Why Flow Matching?
sections.text: The procedure of starting from OPT then turning to the parameterized L ¯ \bar{L} and solving L ′ {L^{\prime}} practically can also be applied to other types of generative models, such as DDPM and score-based models. For example, in DDPM with a parameterized score denoted by s θ s_{\theta} , one can generally replace Assumption 3.2 with a score estimation error in the form 𝔼 t , x t ​ [ ‖ s θ ( λ ) ​ ( x t , t ) − ∇ log ⁡ p ( λ ) ​ ( x t , t ) ‖ 2 2 ] ≤ ν 2 \mathbb{E}_{t,x_{t}}\left[\|s^{{(\lambda)}}_{\theta}(x_{t},t)-\nabla\log p^{(\lambda)}(x_{t},t)\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq\nu^{2} , leading to a similar conclusion of bounded TV as in Lemma D.1 shown in Li and Yan [2025] . As for practically computing the gradient for P s θ ​ ( 𝒞 ) P_{s_{\theta}}{(\mathcal{C})} , one can apply FM-RE’s [ Huan et al., 2026 ] optimization framework due to DDPM’s inherent stochasticity. However, DDPM’s fixed stochasticity, especially the large noise steps at the start of the sampling trajectory, together with hard binary feedback in the FM-RE framework, make the optimization hard to perform in practice. Empirical evidence shows that this approach is able to deal with simple constraints, e.g., ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -ball constraints in Sec. 5.2 , but may induce degraded distribution when the complexity of the constraint increases. In contrast, the FM framework provides more stable sampling trajectories, thereby being able to adapt to more complex constraints while preserving the distributional fidelity with the optimization strategy in Sec. 4.2 .

sections.heading: I.2 Implementation Tips and Relationship with FM-RE
sections.text: From an implementation perspective, a single PDFM iteration with fixed λ ′ = λ / w \lambda^{\prime}=\lambda/w is closely related to FM-RE, if the dual variable in PDFM is interpreted as the weight of the constraint-aware term in FM-RE. Although the procedures for estimating ∇ θ P u θ ​ ( 𝒞 ) \nabla_{\theta}P_{u_{\theta}}(\mathcal{C}) differ, both methods share the same underlying idea: they provide feedback to u θ ​ ( x t , t ) u_{\theta}(x_{t},t) that is explicitly or implicitly derived from the terminal binary feasibility feedback. Since FM-RE requires sampling complete trajectories to obtain terminal oracle feedback, a natural question is whether PDFM also requires complete trajectory sampling during its updates. Only partially. PDFM maintains both u θ u_{\theta} and f ϕ f_{\phi} during the primal update. Training f ϕ f_{\phi} requires complete trajectory sampling, since the terminal oracle value y = 𝟏 𝒞 ​ ( x 1 ) y=\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}}(x_{1}) serves as the training label for the intermediate predictions f ϕ ​ ( x t , t ) f_{\phi}(x_{t},t) . However, complete trajectory sampling is not strictly required to compute grad θ \mathrm{grad}_{\theta} in ( 18 ), because the feedback is provided directly by the fixed estimator f ϕ f_{\phi} . One subtlety is that evaluating ( 18 ) still requires samples of the intermediate x i ​ Δ ​ t x_{i\Delta t} . From an implementation perspective, these states can be approximated using random couplings and linear interpolants, i.e., x i ​ Δ ​ t = ( 1 − i ​ Δ ​ t ) ​ x 0 + i ​ Δ ​ t ​ x 1 x_{i\Delta t}=(1-i\Delta t)x_{0}+i\Delta tx_{1} , provided that the probability path does not deviate significantly, as in the PDE-constrained and molecule generation tasks. Note that f ϕ f_{\phi} , which is fundamentally trained as a classifier, is generally cheaper to train than the more complex velocity field u θ u_{\theta} and does not require highly accurate prediction to provide useful feedback. Since PDFM does not require complete trajectory sampling for the θ \theta -update, it has a computational advantage over FM-RE. In single-iteration evaluations for i > 0 i>0 , PDFM training is approximately 2 2 – 3 × 3\times faster than FM-RE; for example, the runtime is about 1.5 1.5 minutes vs. 4 4 minutes for the 8 8 -D ℓ 2 \ell_{2} ball constraint, and 25 25 minutes vs. 70 70 minutes for Case 1 in Sec. 5.3 . Users seeking faster training can repeat multiple θ \theta -updates between the ϕ \phi -updates, provided that these θ \theta -updates do not substantially change the constraint satisfaction behavior.

sections.heading: I.3 Limitations
sections.text: The limitations of PDFM are summarized as follows: 1. Since f ϕ f_{\phi} is fundamentally trained as a classifier, it requires both positive and negative feedback. Highly imbalanced feedback, especially when the feedback is overwhelmingly negative, meaning that most samples generated by the current u θ u_{\theta} violate the constraint, can prevent f ϕ f_{\phi} from learning reliable decision boundaries and lead to inaccurate feedback. Therefore, at the start of iteration i = 1 i=1 in Alg. 2 , PDFM requires the current velocity field to generate at least some feasible samples. 2. PDFM requires the feasible region to be sufficiently represented or reachable under the data and model distributions. This means one cannot generally expect PDFM to learn a near-optimal constrained distribution when Q Q deviates significantly from 𝒞 \mathcal{C} . In such cases, the FM objective can become severely misaligned with the constraint satisfaction objective, leading to a large optimization error in Assumption 4.3 . sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The theoretical and empirical claims in the abstract match the content in the main text. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Limitations are discussed in detail in Appendix I . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The assumptions are provided in the main text, with detailed proofs provided in the appendix. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The code is released. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).
